q-118712.name: Question 1
q-118712.worked_solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{(x+1)+1}{x+1})}^{2x+2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{2(x+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x+1=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{2(x+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{2n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Evaluate limx→∞(x+2x+1)2x+2.

a
e2
b
e2
c
1e2

2e

Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that as x→∞,

  • the expression inside the parentheses approaches 1, while

  • the exponent approaches ∞.

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

limx→∞(x+2x+1)2x+2=1∞, which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit: limn→∞(1+1n)n=e

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

limx→∞(x+2x+1)2x+2=limx→∞((x+1)+1x+1)2x+2=limx→∞(1+1x+1)2(x+1)

Let x+1=n. Therefore, since n→∞ as x→∞, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows: limx→∞(x+2x+1)2x+2=limx→∞(1+1x+1)2(x+1)=limn→∞(1+1n)2n=limn→∞[(1+1n)n]2=[limn→∞(1+1n)n]2=e2

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3x})}^{2(3x)}\end{aligned}

q-118721.name: Question 3
q-118721.worked_solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{(2x-2)+1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})}^{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $2(x-1)=n$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-1) & =n \\ x-1 & =\frac{n}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n/2} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/2} \\  & ={e}^{1/2} \\  & =\sqrt{e}\end{aligned}
$$

q-127543.name: Question 4
q-127543.worked_solution:
Notice that as $t\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3t-6})}^{t-2}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

In the given limit, we let $3t-6=n.$ Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3t-6 & =n \\ 3(t-2) & =n \\ t-2 & =\frac{n}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3t-6})}^{t-2} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n/3} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/3} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/3} \\  & ={e}^{1/3} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{e}\end{aligned}
$$

q-338566.worked_solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{3}{x})}^{2x}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

In the given limit, we let $\frac{3}{x}=\frac{1}{n}.$ Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{x} & =\frac{1}{n} \\ x & =3n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{3}{x})}^{2x} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{2(3n)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{6} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{6} \\  & ={e}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$
